passage: A year after the car accident, I can drive past that junction again. I'm Jasleen, and I want to say how I got here, because it wasn't by forcing myself. First I made my room feel safe: a lamp by the bed, the door I could lock. I kept small routines, the same morning walk, chai at seven, calling Nani on Sundays. I didn't tell everyone the story; I told two friends what I was ready to say, and nothing more. Then I found a therapist, Manoj, who was trained in trauma. We went slowly. I still remember the crash. Some nights it still comes back. But it doesn't grab me by the throat any more. It's a memory now, not a place I live.

qa.a: A lamp.

qa.a: Jasleen feels calmer and freer, still remembering it but no longer gripped by fear.

qa.q: Which steps helped Jasleen recover gently?
qa.a: Making the room feel safe, keeping routines, sharing only what felt right with two friends and working slowly with a trained therapist.

qa.a: Manoj likely sees that the memory is still there but has lost its grip, which is what recovery looks like.

passage:
Warden's note, men's hostel, Block B.
Shankar, twenty, moved in here three months ago after the fire at his old paying-guest house. At first he slept with the lights on and jumped at every door bang. I've watched how he has handled things. He asked for a ground-floor room near the exit, which we gave him. He keeps a strict routine: gym at six, classes, dinner at eight, lights off at eleven. When the boys asked what happened, he said, "A fire. I'll talk more someday," and left it there. He sees a trauma therapist at the city hospital every Thursday.
This week there was a fire drill. He walked out calmly with everyone else. Afterwards he told me, "I still remember everything. It just doesn't take over." — Sarita

qa.a: He sees his trauma therapist every Thursday.

qa.a: He seemed calm and steady, walking out with everyone else instead of panicking.

qa.a: Asking for a room near the exit, keeping a strict routine, sharing only what he wanted and seeing a trained trauma therapist.

qa.a: They may see him as steady and strong, respecting that he shares his story in his own time.

passage:
Saturday
Today we drove past the place where the bus crashed last year. I told Bhupen before we left, "I might go quiet." He just nodded.
My hands got cold. I looked at the broken railing, now fixed, and I felt sad. But I didn't freeze. I didn't need to get out of the car.
A year ago I couldn't even hear a horn without shaking. What changed? My therapist says it's the small things: sleeping in the same room with the window I trust, dinner at the same time with Ma, telling people only what I'm ready to. And every Tuesday, her room with the green chair, where I can say anything.
I'll never forget the crash. But today it felt like it was behind me.
Pradeep

It's been eight months since Jeevan's mother died. At first he cried, then he started coming back to class. But these last weeks he's stopped attending, stopped eating in the mess, sleeps all day. Today he said, "I'm worthless without her. I don't want to live."

Then, with his okay, I called his elder sister, who's driving over tonight, and the warden came up. I'm still in the corridor outside his door, writing this.
Tomorrow at ten we're going to the counselling centre together. Grief and depression can come together, the helpline person said.
Lakshmi

Over several sessions I've learnt that for months he has kept strict food rules: the same few foods at exactly the same times, and skipping meals entirely before exams. When the mess changed its menu last week, he panicked and didn't eat that day.
He told me, "When everything else is out of control, this is the one thing I can control. It makes me feel calm for a bit." Then he admitted he feels dizzy, cold and ashamed most days.
I told him this relief is real but so is the harm, and that this needs a doctor first. With his agreement, I booked him with the college doctor and informed his parents. — Gargi

Thursday
Exam week. I did the rules again today. Same breakfast, nothing till evening, then only what's on the list. It makes the panic about exams go quiet for a while, like I'm in charge of something.
But I was dizzy on the stairs. My hands are always cold. I hide what I'm doing, even from Lalit, and he's my brother, I tell him everything.
Tonight Lalit sat at the end of my bed. He said, "I've noticed you're not eating with us. I'm not angry. I'm scared for you." I cried and told him some of it.
He said, "This isn't something you can fix alone." He's right. Tomorrow we're going to the doctor together. I've already told Mummy.
Arohi

Dear Minakshi,
You told me you've been avoiding the mirror and scrolling fitness pages all night. I get it more than you think. At nineteen, I used to hate every photo of myself.
A few things helped me. I muted every account that made me feel small. I started eating three proper meals, not skipping. I swam, and I started noticing what my body could do instead of how it looked: forty lengths, then sixty. When I caught myself saying something cruel about my body, I tried saying something kind instead, even if it felt silly.
But I'll be honest. When mine got serious, I needed a doctor and a counsellor. If it's taking over your day, please tell Masi, and we'll find someone. I'll come with you.
Vishal
